titre: Kant, 1784: Enlightenment, Public Reason, and Obedience
accroche: Kant asks that we dare to think for ourselves, and yet accepts that one should obey without arguing in one's post: everything depends on who is speaking, and to whom.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the December 1783 issue of a Berlin monthly, the Berlinische Monatsschrift, a footnote poses, without answering it, a question: what is Enlightenment, Aufklärung? It is by the pastor Johann Friedrich Zöllner, and it extends a debate about marriage: should one stop calling on the clergy to perform it? Moses Mendelssohn answers in September 1784. Kant signs his answer in Königsberg on September 30; it appears in the same monthly in December 1784 (pp. 481-494). He writes it without having read Mendelssohn's: a note specifies that it has not yet reached him.

## Emerging from Immaturity

Kant's answer fits in one sentence: Enlightenment is what brings man out of “the immaturity for which he is himself responsible” (translation by Jules Barni, 1853). Immaturity is the inability to use one's understanding without being directed by another. It stems, Kant says, from laziness and cowardice: “It is so convenient to be immature!” A book thinks for me, a spiritual director has a conscience for me, a doctor judges my diet for me. Hence the motto: sapere aude, have the courage to use your own understanding.

## The Side That Is Quoted Less

One would expect from this program a distrust of all authority. Kant sets a precise limit on it. He reports the cries of the day: the officer says “do not argue, but carry out orders,” the financier “do not argue, but pay,” the priest “do not argue, but believe.” He does not reject them wholesale. He distinguishes two uses of reason. The public use is the one made “as a scholar, before the entire reading public”: it must always be free. The private use is the one made in “a certain civil post or office”: it may be very narrowly restricted, without greatly hindering the progress of enlightenment.

In this vocabulary, “private” does not mean personal. The priest who speaks to his parishioners makes a private use of his reason, since he is carrying out someone else's commission. The officer who receives an order “must obey” and must not argue aloud while on duty. The citizen cannot refuse to pay taxes. But the officer, as a scholar, can write about the faults of military service and submit his remarks to the public, the priest can criticize his Church, the citizen can publish what he thinks of taxes.

## An Age of Enlightenment, Not an Enlightened Age

Kant does not claim that his time has reached the goal. To the question “do we live today in an enlightened age?”, he answers: “no, but we do live in an age of enlightenment.” He calls this age that of Frederick, a prince who considers it a duty to prescribe nothing to men in matters of religion. And he notes that only a prince who has at hand “a numerous and perfectly disciplined army” can say what a republic would not dare say: argue as much as you like, only obey.

The freedom he asks for here is the freedom to publish; nowhere does he write that it authorizes disobedience in one's office. It is the condition of progress, and Kant holds it compatible with obedience in one's office. What remains to be seen is what becomes of this distinction when the reading public is no longer a circle of the learned.

carte.punch: Kant, 1784: Enlightenment is an emergence from immaturity, not a right to disobey.
carte.idee: Kant distinguishes the public use of reason, which must always be free, from the private use, that of an officer or a priest in his office, which may be narrowly restricted. The freedom he defends here is the freedom to publish.

quiz.question: When Kant writes that the “private” use of reason may be very narrowly restricted, what is he talking about?
choix: The reason exercised in a post or office, like that of the officer or the priest
Intimate thought, which no power reaches but which no one needs to express
Reasoning carried on within the family or among friends, too unserious to be free
The reflection of a scholar who writes for colleagues rather than for the general public
quiz.explication: For Kant, “private” designates the exercise of reason in an entrusted office: the officer must obey the order, the priest follows his Church's creed before his parishioners. Intimate thought and conversation among friends are not his subject. And the scholar who publishes addresses the “entire reading public”: that is precisely the public use, which must always be free.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who posed, in a 1783 footnote, the question “what is Enlightenment” to which Kant answers in 1784?
choix: Moses Mendelssohn, in his own answer published in September 1784
Frederick II of Prussia, in a decree on freedom of worship
Kant himself, in the introduction to his December 1784 answer
The pastor Johann Friedrich Zöllner, in a debate on civil marriage
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The note is by the pastor Zöllner, inserted in a debate on civil marriage. Mendelssohn merely answers afterward, in September 1784, and Kant answers in turn without having yet read his. Frederick II appears in the entry only as a figure of the age, not as the author of the question.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Kant say that “it is so convenient to be immature”?
choix: Because the laws of the state explicitly forbid thinking for oneself in most matters
Because a book thinks for us, a spiritual director stands in for our conscience, a doctor judges our diet
Because the Church has taken away from individuals the right to read and interpret sacred texts
Because the public use of reason is, according to Kant, always harder than the private use
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kant describes immaturity as a comfort: a book thinks in one's place, a spiritual director stands in for one's conscience, a doctor judges one's diet. He invokes no law forbidding thought, nor the Church, nor any difficulty peculiar to the public use.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, in what case does an officer remain free to criticize military service publicly?
choix: Never, military obedience excludes any criticism, even published under his name
When his superior expressly authorizes him to speak on the subject
When he writes as a scholar, to submit his remarks to the reading public
When he has left the army and is no longer subject to any hierarchical order
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that “the officer, as a scholar, can write about the faults of military service and submit his remarks to the public”: this is the public use of reason, always free, distinct from the obedience he owes in his post.
